words.shortDefinition: A serving pattern that routes a request through multiple models in sequence or parallel and combines their outputs — supported natively by Triton and KServe.
words.simpleDefinition: Instead of one model per prediction, ensemble serving routes each request through multiple models — perhaps a pre-processor, several specialized predictors, and a combiner — executing the pipeline entirely server-side as a single logical call. The client sees one endpoint; the server orchestrates the multi-model pipeline transparently.
words.longDefinition: Model ensemble serving operationalizes the ML ensemble pattern in a production serving context. Rather than requiring the client application to orchestrate multiple model calls, the model server defines a pipeline that chains models together declaratively, executes them server-side with minimal inter-model data transfer overhead, and returns a single response. NVIDIA Triton's Ensemble Scheduler is the most mature implementation: models are connected via a DAG defined in a config.pbtxt where each model's output tensors map to another model's input tensors. Triton executes the DAG on the server, transferring tensors between models via GPU shared memory (no serialization or network hop between stages). KServe implements a similar concept through its Transformer-Predictor-Explainer pipeline and through its Graph InferenceGraph CRD for multi-model DAGs. Ensemble patterns in production include: preprocessing ensembles (tokenizer model → embedding model → downstream model), heterogeneous ensembles (three specialized models whose logits are averaged by a meta-learner), cascade ensembles (fast model for most requests, slow model called only on uncertain cases), and modality fusion ensembles (text model + image model → fusion model for multimodal inputs). Ensemble serving must address failure handling — when one model in the DAG fails or times out, the overall ensemble must have a defined fallback or error behavior rather than silently returning a partial result.
words.connector: Think of model ensemble serving like a relay race where the baton passes between specialist runners — each model stage runs its leg, passes its output directly to the next, and the system presents just the final result to the watching crowd.
words.techContext: Our search ranking system uses Triton ensemble serving: a BERT embedding model, a candidate retrieval model, and a ranking model are chained in a single Triton ensemble pipeline, eliminating three network hops and reducing end-to-end latency by 45% versus client-side orchestration.
words.exampleSentence: Migrating from client-side multi-model orchestration to Triton ensemble serving eliminated 40 ms of network serialization overhead per request — in our 100 ms SLA system, that saved us from needing an additional GPU node to meet latency targets.
words.etymology: Ensemble from French ensemble ('together'); serving in the ML deployment sense; the compound model ensemble serving describes the operationalized production form of the ML ensemble learning technique, adapted for real-time inference infrastructure.

words.shortDefinition: The MLOps lifecycle for managing fine-tuned LLM adapter variants: versioning LoRA weights, tracking fine-tuning datasets, evaluating adapted model quality, and serving multiple adapters from a shared base.
words.simpleDefinition: Fine-tuning operations applies full MLOps discipline to the production lifecycle of fine-tuned models: versioning the adapter weights and the dataset used to create them, running eval harnesses to validate quality before promotion, serving multiple adapter variants from a single base model in production, and monitoring per-adapter metrics to detect drift.
words.longDefinition: Fine-tuning operations (sometimes FineTune Ops or FT-Ops) addresses the unique operational challenges that arise when organizations maintain fleets of fine-tuned model variants derived from a shared base model. Unlike classical MLOps where each model is independent, fine-tuned systems have a hierarchical artifact structure: the base model (a massive, rarely-changing foundation), adapter weights (small, frequently updated delta parameters), and fine-tuning datasets (often proprietary, requiring careful versioning and access control). The operational lifecycle has several LLM-specific dimensions: dataset curation and deduplication pipelines (fine-tuning data quality has outsized impact on outcome), adapter versioning in a model registry with lineage linking each adapter version to its dataset version and base model version, evaluation workflows that test adapted models against task-specific eval suites (not just general benchmarks), multi-adapter serving infrastructure that can serve dozens or hundreds of LoRA adapters from a single base model instance using dynamic adapter loading (LoRAX, PEFT's adapter switching, vLLM adapter support), and per-adapter monitoring that tracks how each adapter's quality metrics drift independently over time. The promotion workflow for adapters mirrors software CI/CD: a new adapter version enters an eval pipeline, passes behavioral and safety checks, and is promoted to production via a rollout strategy. Rollback is adapter-level — reverting to a previous adapter version restores behavior without touching the base model.
words.connector: Think of fine-tuning operations like managing a franchise restaurant chain where each location (adapter) has its own local menu (task specialization) derived from the corporate recipe book (base model) — you need version control for both the corporate recipes and each location's adaptations.
words.techContext: We use LoRAX to serve 200 customer-specific LoRA adapters on a pool of three Llama-3 8B base model instances, with adapter promotion gated by an eval harness that must show >0.85 judge score before any adapter reaches production traffic.
words.exampleSentence: Fine-tuning operations discipline prevented a bad adapter from reaching production when our eval harness caught a 22% safety policy violation rate on a hastily fine-tuned customer-specific variant — a failure invisible to the training loss metric.

words.shortDefinition: An open-source data versioning and pipeline platform that attaches data provenance to every pipeline step, automatically detecting when upstream data changes require downstream recomputation.
words.simpleDefinition: Pachyderm is a data-centric workflow platform that treats datasets the way Git treats source code — every data commit is versioned, every pipeline step is linked to the exact input data version it consumed, and when upstream data changes, Pachyderm automatically re-runs only the downstream steps that are affected.
words.longDefinition: Pachyderm (the open-source project) combines two conceptually linked capabilities: a data versioning layer (PFS — Pachyderm File System) built on top of object storage with Git-like commit semantics, and a pipeline orchestration layer that enforces strict input-output data provenance. PFS gives each dataset state a unique, immutable commit ID. When data is updated, a new commit is created rather than overwriting the existing state, preserving the full history of every dataset version. Pipelines in Pachyderm are containerized transformations that declare their input repositories explicitly; when a new commit arrives on an input repository, Pachyderm automatically triggers the pipeline, runs the transformation, and creates a new output commit. This automatic incremental processing means that if only 1,000 new images are added to a training dataset of 1 million, only those 1,000 new images flow through the pipeline — not the full dataset. The provenance graph — which pipeline run consumed which input commits to produce which output commits — is recorded automatically and queryable via API. For ML use cases, this means every trained model artifact has a complete, verifiable lineage: the exact data commits, code version, and hyperparameters that produced it. Pachyderm integrates with Kubernetes (pipelines run as Kubernetes Jobs), major cloud object stores (S3, GCS, Azure Blob), and MLflow. It is particularly well-suited for regulated industries (healthcare, finance) where reproducibility and audit are requirements rather than nice-to-haves.
words.connector: Think of Pachyderm like a version-controlled assembly line in manufacturing — every time raw materials change, the line automatically re-processes only the affected batches, and every finished product has a complete bill of materials traceable to the exact inputs used.
words.techContext: Our medical imaging pipeline uses Pachyderm to ensure every model is retrained only when the underlying annotated dataset changes, with automatic provenance linking each model version to the exact imaging data commit — a regulatory requirement for our FDA submission.
words.exampleSentence: Pachyderm's automatic incremental processing reduced our nightly retraining pipeline runtime from 6 hours to 25 minutes by processing only the 3,000 new annotated images rather than the full 2-million-image corpus on every run.

codeExample.code:
# Pachyderm pipeline spec: train model when data changes
pipeline:
  name: train-classifier
description: "Retrain on new labeled images"
transform:
  image: myrepo/training-image:v3
  cmd: ["python", "train.py"]
  env:
    EPOCHS: "20"
input:
  pfs:
    repo: labeled-images      # triggers on new commits
    glob: "/*"
resource_requests:
  gpu:
    type: nvidia.com/gpu
    number: 1
output_branch: master

words.etymology: Pachyderm is named after the thick-skinned mammal order (elephants, rhinos) — chosen because 'Pachyderm never forgets', a play on the elephant's reputation for long memory, applied to the platform's promise of complete data history retention; founded in 2014.
